title: Clock, days, and time
goal: Tell the time correctly — including the Icelandic half hour, which counts toward the next hour and trips English speakers up for life.
bekal: ask and tell the time, including "past" and "to"
name the days, the months, and everyday time expressions

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hvað er klukkan?
dialogs.intro: In the school hallway, a few minutes before class. Búdí panics about the time, then discovers that one part of Icelandic is something he has known since childhood.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Æ, nei! Tíminn byrjar hálf fjögur.
lines.id: Oh no! Class starts at half past three.
lines.literal: oh, no! class-the begins half four.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Þá höfum við fimmtán mínútur. Nóg af tíma.
lines.id: Then we have fifteen minutes. Plenty of time.
lines.literal: then have we fifteen minutes. enough of time.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: „Hálf fjögur" — af hverju fjögur? Klukkan er þrjú!
lines.id: "Hálf fjögur" — why four? It's three o'clock!
lines.literal: half four — of what four? clock-the is three!

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Af því að hálftíminn er á leiðinni í fjögur.
lines.id: Because the half hour is on its way to four.
lines.literal: of that that half-hour-the is on way-the to four.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Æ, það er eins og á indónesísku! „Setengah empat".
lines.id: Oh, it's just like in Indonesian! "Setengah empat".
lines.literal: oh, it is one and in Indonesian! half four.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Sannarlega? Þá ertu heppinn. Enskumælandi fólk ruglast alltaf.
lines.id: Really? Then you're lucky. English speakers always get confused.
lines.literal: truly? then are-you lucky. English-speaking people get-confused always.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Á morgun er enginn tími. Það er laugardagur.
lines.id: There's no class tomorrow. It's Saturday.
lines.literal: on morning is no class. it is Saturday.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.id: Of course! So what shall we do?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Við förum í sund klukkan tíu og borðum svo hádegismat.
lines.id: We'll go swimming at ten and then have lunch.
lines.literal: we go to swimming at ten and eat then midday-food.

notes: **Hálf fjögur means 3:30, not 4:30.** Icelandic counts **toward** the next hour — "half to four" — just like German *halb vier* and Búdí's Indonesian *setengah empat*. English speakers trip over this for life, because British "half four" means 4:30. Read *hálf* + hour as "halfway to" that hour.

**Klukkan is called hún**, because *klukka* is kvenkyn. That's why the answer is *Hún er þrjú*, not *Það er þrjú*. It's the use of noun gender from Unit 3 that you'll say most often, every single day.
**Korter yfir / korter í** — "a quarter past" and "a quarter to". The word *korter* was borrowed from Danish and is one of the few loanwords that survive in everyday Icelandic.

**Á morgun means "tomorrow", not "in the morning".** Compare three similar forms: *á morgun* (tomorrow), *í morgun* (this morning, earlier), *á morgnana* (every morning). One letter apart, three different times — learn all three together. (English has a similar pair: *morning* and *tomorrow*.)

**Laugardagur literally means "bath day".** *Laug* means a hot pool — the same word as in *sundlaug* in Unit 7. In the saga age, Saturday really was bath day, and the name has survived to this day. Almost all the Icelandic day names hold history like this.
**Hádegismatur literally means "midday food".** *Hádegi* = the high point of the day. You can take it apart yourself, and that's how most Icelandic compounds work.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: One pattern for "past", one for "to", and one for the half hour. The hour number always uses the **hvorugkyn** form (*eitt*, *tvö*, *þrjú*, *fjögur*).
after: **Yfir** for "past", **í** for "to". The turning point is minute 30: after the half hour, Icelanders count down to the next hour, just as English says "a quarter to four".
To say when something happens, put *klukkan* in front: *Tíminn byrjar **klukkan** þrjú.* The word *klukkan* can't be dropped — it also signals that you're giving a time, not a quantity.
In official writing and timetables, Iceland uses the 24-hour clock: *17.30*, read *sautján þrjátíu*. In conversation, people still say *hálf sex*.

grammars.title: Days and months
body: All the day names are **karlkyn** and end in *-dagur*. Month names are karlkyn too, and all are written in **lowercase** — unlike in English.
after: To say "on …day", use **á** + the þágufall form: *á mánudaginn* (this Monday), *á mánudögum* (on Mondays). Singular versus plural is what separates a one-off from a habit.
The months: *janúar, febrúar, mars, apríl, maí, júní, júlí, ágúst, september, október, nóvember, desember* — you can guess almost all of them. For "in …" use *í*: *í júlí*.

blocks.title: Three forms one letter apart
items: **á morgun** = tomorrow. **í morgun** = this morning (earlier). **á morgnana** = every morning. All three come from the word *morgunn* (morning), and all three are very common — so picking the wrong one gets noticed fast.
The same pattern repeats: **í** for what has already passed today (*í morgun*, *í gær*), **á** for what's coming or what repeats (*á morgun*, *á morgnana*).

rows: Eigum við að segja hálf níu?
AY-ghüm vidh ahdh SEH-yah howlv NEE-ü

blocks.text: *Eigum við að segja …?* literally means "shall we say …?" and is used just like English "how about …?". It's one of the most useful phrases for arranging anything.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right day of the week.
items: The day in the middle of the week is ____.
____ (Í morgun, Á morgun) fer ég í skólann klukkan átta — það er á miðvikudaginn.
____ (Í gær, Í dag) var laugardagur; í dag er sunnudagur.
Ég vakna klukkan sjö ____ (á morgnana, á morgun).
Við hittumst ____ (í kvöld, í nótt) klukkan átta.
Ég drakk kaffi ____ (í morgun, á morgun) klukkan sex.
Class starts at half past three.

answers: Klukkan er tvö. — Korter yfir fimm. — Hálf átta. — Korter í tíu. — Tíu mínútur yfir ellefu. — Hálf tvö.
Á morgun — Í gær — á morgnana — í kvöld — í morgun
Hvað er klukkan? — Korter yfir þrjú. — Tíminn byrjar hálf fjögur. — Á morgun er laugardagur. — Hvenær hittumst við? — Hentar þér klukkan sjö?
